name: Serpentine Green
lede: Serpentine Green is a dark, dulled yellow-green named for serpentine, a usually green rock whose own name comes from its mottled, scaly resemblance to a serpent's skin, not from its color.

sections.title: A rock, not a snake
sections.body:
The serpentine group is a family of minerals, usually green, that make up the rock geologists call serpentinite; both words trace to the Latin *serpentinus*, "resembling a serpent," for the rock's mottled, scaly surface rather than for any one color [3]. Fresh serpentinite ranges from soft yellow-green through rich emerald to nearly black, so no single swatch can stand for the stone, and this particular dark, muted tone is just one point in that range [3].

Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists this hue on plate XVI, hue 23′, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS 1955 revision calls the block "light olive" [1][2]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the English name to 1912, the same year as Ridgway's own atlas [1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 55, chroma 35, hue 102, close to [[dull-citrine|Dull Citrine]] and to [[parrot-green|Parrot Green]] and [[warbler-green|Warbler Green]] elsewhere in the library [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A screen match for this green turns up in 659 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.8 percent, as photographed [2]. Paulus Potter, a Dutch painter known for cattle and pasture scenes, carries it nearly thirteen times above the archive's average rate, and its single largest appearance is a 1700 Indian depiction of Shiva, where it covers nearly two-thirds of the canvas [2]. The match is a computed color on an aged, varnished painting, never a claim about the actual pigment used [2].

questions.q: The word "serpentine" describes the mineral's name because of its:
choices: Its shape when cut into beads

questions.q: True or false: all serpentine mineral is the exact same shade of green.

openers: Serpentine is named for its snakeskin texture, not for any single color — the real mineral ranges from yellow-green to nearly black.
